values.meaning: The chain stops at something that could not have failed to exist.
values.examples: Classical theism (Aquinas); Spinoza's substance; Platonism about mathematics; Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason.

values.meaning: The chain stops at something that simply is, with no reason.
values.examples: Russell ("the universe is just there, and that's all"); Hume; most default physicalism.

values.meaning: The chain never stops: infinite regress, or a loop.
values.examples: Infinite nested simulations (the owner's Infinite Box Cascade run forever); cyclic cosmologies; Buddhist dependent origination read cosmologically; Hegel's self-grounding Absolute read as a loop.

values.meaning: Statable in mathematics, physics, or reasoning we have, whether or not we can test it yet.
values.examples: Physicalism; mathematical universe; simulation hypothesis; most theisms that ascribe properties to God.

values.value: Graspable by some mind, not ours
values.meaning: Describable in a logic that a differently built mind could hold, but closed to human cognition.
values.examples: McGinn's cognitive closure; Chomsky's "mysteries"; the owner's Fog Front in its position-relative sense.

values.meaning: Not describable in any logic at all.
values.examples: Apophatic theology (Pseudo-Dionysius); Neoplatonic One beyond being; Nirguna Brahman; the Dao that cannot be spoken; Kant's noumenon in its strongest reading; the owner's Un-Concept in its strongest sense.

values.value: Authored by an agent in a higher layer
values.meaning: A being inside a larger physical reality made ours.
values.examples: Simulation hypothesis (Bostrom); the owner's Sandbox / Architect; Gnostic demiurge; Plato's Timaeus craftsman.

values.value: Authored by an agent identical to the ground
values.meaning: The terminal ground is itself a mind that willed our layer.
values.examples: Classical theism; Berkeley's idealism; Kastrup's analytic idealism read theistically.

values.meaning: The observers inside the layer are, collectively or ultimately, its authors.
values.examples: Wheeler's participatory universe; some readings of Advaita (Brahman = Atman); self-simulation hypotheses.

values.meaning: Our layer had to exist as it is.
values.examples: Necessitarianism; Spinoza; some block-universe readings; Tegmark's mathematical universe (all consistent structures exist).

values.meaning: Our layer just exists, no reason.
values.examples: Default physicalism; Russell.

values.meaning: Our layer is one of many, and we find ourselves in this one for anthropic or evolutionary reasons.
values.examples: Multiverse plus anthropic principle; Smolin's cosmological natural selection; eternal inflation; the owner's "multi-universal evolution."

C.name: What kind of thing is fundamental?

values.meaning: The ground is mind-like. Matter is what mind looks like from outside, or is a pattern in mind.
values.examples: Idealism (Berkeley, Kastrup); cosmopsychism (Goff, Shani); Advaita Vedanta; Yogācāra Buddhism; the owner's "feeling is the very thing from the start" (Turn 7).

values.meaning: The ground is physical: particles, fields, spacetime, or whatever physics bottoms out in. Experience is derived or illusory.
values.examples: Physicalism; materialism; the owner's Clutter / AI pillar.

values.meaning: The ground is mathematical or informational structure. Physical stuff is what structure looks like when instantiated, or structure is all there is.
values.examples: Tegmark's mathematical universe; Wheeler's "it from bit"; digital physics (Zuse, Fredkin); ontic structural realism (Ladyman); the owner's Universe Code pillar.

values.meaning: The ground is neither mental nor physical but gives rise to both.
values.examples: Neutral monism (Russell, James, Mach); dual-aspect monism (Spinoza on one reading; Pauli–Jung); Russellian monism (which is sometimes filed as C1).

values.meaning: More than one fundamental kind, irreducible to each other.
values.examples: Substance dualism (Descartes); property dualism (Chalmers); Samkhya's Purusha and Prakriti; Cartesian interactionism.

S.name: What is the author's stance toward us?

values.meaning: Has no attitude toward inhabitants; we are side effects or data.
values.examples: Bostrom's ancestor simulations run for research; the owner's "indifferent engineer watching data points"; Epicurean gods; deism.

values.meaning: Wants inhabitants' good, as inhabitants would understand good.
values.examples: Classical theism (omnibenevolence); Bahá'í; most Abrahamic mainstream.

values.meaning: Wants inhabitants' harm.
values.examples: Gnostic demiurge (in some readings); Descartes' evil demon as hypothesis; "dystheism."

values.meaning: Has attitudes, but they do not map onto human good and evil.
values.examples: The owner's Architect in Turn 12 ("emotion or something similar ... not rooted in survival so don't see evil good ... the same way"); Lovecraftian cosmicism; the Hebrew Bible's God on some critical readings; Hindu deities with both creative and destructive aspects.

values.meaning: We cannot determine the stance, or (under B2b) no stance can be asserted.
values.examples: Negative theology; Job's conclusion; agnostic theism.

values.meaning: Moral facts are grounded in the nature or will of the terminal ground.
values.examples: Divine command theory; natural law (Aquinas); Platonic Form of the Good; Dharma as cosmic order.

values.meaning: Moral facts are natural facts (about welfare, flourishing, cooperation), discoverable empirically.
values.examples: Cornell realism (Boyd, Sturgeon); Railton; Aristotle on one reading; Harris's Moral Landscape.

values.meaning: Moral facts are real, mind-independent, but not natural or supernatural; known by intuition or reason.
values.examples: Moore; Parfit (On What Matters); Enoch; Huemer.

values.meaning: Moral claims aim at facts and all are false.
values.examples: Mackie (1977); Joyce.

values.meaning: Moral claims do not aim at facts; they express attitudes.
values.examples: Ayer; Blackburn; Gibbard.

values.meaning: Moral facts exist but are constructed by agents' rational or contractual activity.
values.examples: Kant (on one reading); Rawls; Korsgaard; Scanlon.

values.meaning: Moral truth is relative to a culture or framework.
values.examples: Harman; Wong; folk relativism.

values.meaning: Outcomes.
values.examples: Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill, Singer); effective altruism; negative utilitarianism.

values.meaning: Duties, rules, rights.

values.meaning: Character and flourishing.
values.examples: Aristotle; Confucius; MacIntyre; Stoicism.

values.meaning: What rational agents would agree to.

values.meaning: Relationships and situated response.
values.examples: Noddings; Held; Dancy.

values.examples: Ockham; Adams; Ash'arite theology.

values.meaning: Already tested, result in hand.

rules.title: Eliminate cells, not names
rules.text: A named theory may be eliminated only by eliminating a cell it occupies. If the theory can relocate to a neighboring cell without losing its content, it is not eliminated; it is moved. Record the move.
rules.why: named theories are elastic. "Simulation hypothesis" survives any physics result by adjusting the simulator's capabilities. Only the cell D1a ∧ (specific rendering artifact predicted) is eliminable.

rules.title: Elimination requires an exhaustive partition
rules.text: You may conclude "therefore the remaining cell is true" only if the cells form a partition proven exhaustive by Axiom 1 (excluded middle or a proven finite enumeration). Over a list of names, the conclusion is invalid.
rules.why: the four-pillar version eliminated Code, Sandbox and Clutter and concluded Un-Concept. It missed C1 D2, C4, C5 and A3 entirely (02-genesis.md §6). Over the partition, the same three eliminations leave five live regions, not one.

rules.title: Unexplained is not inexplicable (Axiom 5)
rules.text: A cell is eliminated by a positive result it forbids, or by a proof of internal inconsistency. A cell is never eliminated by the absence of a successful theory within it.
rules.why: the informal game said "if none of the knowable theories explain consciousness, the Un-Concept is proven." That infers F4 from F1/F2 failure. Corollary 2 in 07-fog-front.md shows F4 cannot be proven from any position. Persistent failure raises the credence of F3/F4 and nothing more.

rules.title: Index every knowability claim to a position (Axiom 2)
rules.text: "Unknowable" must read "outside K(p)" with p named. When To Nyn moves, re-check. A claim in F3 at one To Nyn may be F1 at the next.

rules.title: One test, one axis
rules.text: Record for each test which single axis value it bears on and in which direction. A test that "supports simulation" must name the cell (D1a with which sub-property) and the alternative it disfavors. See 09-tests.md columns.

rules.title: Behavior tests never reach experience (Axiom 6)
rules.text: No result of T05, T06, T07 or any emulation, biocomputing or AI benchmark may be recorded as bearing on axis C's experiential content. They may bear on C2-f vs C2-b functional predictions only.

rules.title: Author claims never reach ground claims
rules.text: A result about Layer 2 (D1a author: exists, has stance S) says nothing about axes A and B. Do not propagate upward. The owner's "just another box" is this rule.

rules.title: Value never descends without a bridge (Axiom 7)
rules.text: No genesis result eliminates or establishes an M or N cell without a stated bridging premise. The constraint table in 06-morality.md §4 lists the only propagations currently justified.

rules.title: Record eliminations in the tests registry, dated
rules.text: An elimination is recorded as: cell, test ID, date, result, and the rule under which it counts. Undated eliminations are void.

rules.title: Do not let evaluators score the game (Axiom 9)
rules.text: Praise from an AI system or any single evaluator does not change a cell's status. Only registry entries do.

rules.title: Preserve the eliminated
rules.text: Eliminated cells stay on the map, marked. History of the fog is data (Axiom 10).

glossary.Cognitive closure: Some truths are inaccessible to a mind of a given architecture.
glossary.Noumenon / phenomenon: Things in themselves vs. things as they appear.
glossary.Apophatic / via negativa: Speaking of the ground only by negation.
glossary.Euthyphro dilemma: Is X good because commanded, or commanded because good?
glossary.Is–ought gap: Descriptive premises do not entail normative conclusions.
glossary.Problem of evil (logical / evidential): Inconsistency / improbability of S+ with suffering.
glossary.Free will defense: Suffering as cost of free agency; answers the logical form.
glossary.Evolutionary debunking: Moral beliefs explained by selection, undermining M1c.
glossary.Emergence / effective theory: Higher-level laws not practically deducible from lower.
glossary.Interface theory of perception: Perception evolved for fitness, not truth.
glossary.Simulation argument: Trilemma implying most observers are simulated, given premises.
glossary.Mathematical universe hypothesis: All consistent mathematical structures exist physically.
glossary.Participatory universe: Observers help bring the universe into being.
glossary.Amplituhedron: Geometric object whose volume gives scattering amplitudes in planar N=4 SYM.
glossary.Holographic error correction: Bulk spacetime encoded in boundary via QEC (AdS/CFT toy models).
glossary.Criticality: Brain dynamics near a phase transition.
glossary.Illusionism: Phenomenal consciousness is an introspective illusion.
glossary.Panpsychism / cosmopsychism: Experience is fundamental / the cosmos is the fundamental subject.
glossary.Neutral monism: Ground is neither mental nor physical.
glossary.Analytic idealism: Reality is mind; brains are dissociated alters.
glossary.Gödel incompleteness: Consistent arithmetic-capable systems have unprovable truths.
glossary.Halting problem: No general decision procedure for program termination.
glossary.Pessimistic meta-induction: Past "final" theories were superseded; so will current ones.
glossary.Unconceived alternatives: Elimination fails because live options were never conceived.
glossary.Distributed / extended cognition: Tools and groups are part of the cognitive system.
glossary.Optically pumped magnetometer (OPM): Room-temperature magnetic sensor enabling wearable MEG.
glossary.Inverse problem (MEG/EEG): Non-unique reconstruction of sources from surface fields.
